source.title: When Hardness of Approximation Meets Hardness of Learning

record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically analyzes gradient-descent learning and reports loss outcomes, but on constructed distribution families rather than the benchmark and network settings named in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's gradient-descent theorems and DNF corollary report its own loss results. Results about approximation and correlation queries do not measure gradient-based training and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study proves population hinge-loss and computational lower bounds for constructed distribution families. These results do not test any named version: they measure neither CIFAR training classification error nor the specified effects of width, depth, initialization, learning-rate stability or batch normalization. Safran and Shamir is cited as related work only.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but narrower than the paper's overall conclusion: a single distribution-family variance property yields both approximation and learning hardness results. Its gradient-descent conclusions concern restricted finite-precision or noisy algorithms; the DNF step lower bound depends on the stated initialization, gradient, noise and learning-rate assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical analysis of approximate and noisy gradient descent with hinge loss on constructed distribution families; it does not use the benchmark training recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The guarantees depend on gradient precision, noise, learning rate, step count, initialization constraints, gradient bounds, and family variance.

fits_no_version.finding: For small-variance distribution families, rounded population gradients can leave learning stuck at initialization. Under bounded-noise and small-step assumptions, noisy gradient descent also has a high expected hinge-loss lower bound for some target and distribution, yielding an exponential step lower bound for distribution-free DNF learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite-precision or bounded-noise gradient descent can require very high precision or exponentially many steps to achieve low population hinge loss on certain constructed distribution families.

record.problems: The results are theoretical bounds under restrictive assumptions on the initialization, gradient precision or noise, and gradient norms. They do not report experiments or benchmark classification error.
record.rows_left_out: No gradient-training result rows were left out. Approximation and correlation-query results are outside the claimed gradient-training behavior.

untested.parts: All parts: convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, training classification error, random labels, and model-size or training-recipe comparisons.
All parts: realizable two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
All parts: training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization and normalization-free residual training.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, training speed, trainable depth and orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparisons.
All parts: recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature reduction, divergence and edge-of-stability dynamics.
All parts: batch normalization's effects on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and comparisons with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: High population hinge loss does not by itself establish substantial training classification error or convergence to spurious local minima. These theoretical results therefore warrant no verdict on V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; large convolutional networks; random initialization; SGD or Adam; corrupted or random labels; training classification error; size, early stopping, and regularization comparisons.
No teacher-student two-layer ReLU experiment or neuron-count sweep; Safran and Shamir is cited as prior work.
No plain-versus-residual network depth comparison; no ImageNet or CIFAR-10 experiments; no shortcut or normalization tests.
No initialization comparison or signal/gradient propagation experiment.
No learning-rate stability-limit, curvature, or sharpness experiment.
No batch-normalization comparison or accuracy-speed measurement.

rows.subject: parametric hypothesis class H = {h_w : w ∈ R^N}
rows.size_stated: N parameters; no numerical size stated
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of Δ-approximate gradient descent with hinge loss on a family A of labeled distributions.

conditions.value: w0 sampled from W; almost surely |h_w0(x)| ≤ 1 and ||∇w h_w0(x)|| ≤ B
general family A with variance Var(A)

rows.measure: Expected hinge loss after T gradient-descent steps, with expectation over initialization W.
rows.value: There exists (f,D) ∈ A such that E_W L_f(D)(h_wT) ≥ 3/4(1 − √(8 Var(A))).
rows.note: A theoretical lower bound for a selected distribution pair; not a benchmark training-error measurement. The paper states the conclusion for any T, with the specified approximate-gradient condition.
rows.check: The theoretical hinge-loss lower bound is outside all six versions; it cannot establish their presence or absence. The extracted bound and initialization conditions agree with Theorem 10.

rows.subject: hypothesis class H = {h_w : w ∈ R^N}
rows.size_stated: N parameters; no numerical size stated
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of σ-noisy gradient descent with hinge loss on a family A of labeled distributions.

conditions.value: w0 sampled from W; almost surely |h_w0(x)| ≤ 1/2
Every h_w is differentiable and ||∇w h_w(x)|| ≤ B
general family A with variance Var(A)

rows.measure: Expected hinge loss after T steps, with expectation over initialization and noise.
rows.value: There exists (f,D) ∈ A such that E L_f(D)(h_wT) ≥ 3/4(1 − √(8 Var(A))).
rows.note: A theoretical lower bound for a selected distribution pair under bounded-gradient and noisy-update assumptions.
rows.check: Outside all six versions. The step-count condition is transcribed incorrectly: Theorem 11's proof requires T ≤ Δ²/(32B²N Var(A)), rather than 32B²N/(Δ² Var(A)). Noise is i.i.d., lattice-valued and bounded in norm by σ; the learning-rate restriction is essential.

rows.measure: Number of noisy gradient-descent steps required to approximate f with respect to D.
rows.note: This is a theoretical step lower bound for a selected DNF and distribution, not a measured benchmark error.
rows.check: Outside all six versions. The parameter dependence in the step lower bound is misread: applying Theorem 11 gives 2^{Ω(n^(1/3))} Δ²/(B²N), rather than 2^{Ω(n^(1/3))} B²/(Δ²N). The supplied corollary formula is flattened; this correction follows from Theorem 11's proof. The result also inherits its noise and learning-rate restrictions.
